title: Lourdes and Fatima as pilgrims
hook: the sick and their caregivers at the heart of the pilgrimage

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Holy Land, the ground some people call the fifth gospel, and everyone who lives on it. Your line was the fifth gospel. Which Gospel scene did you find on a map? Day one thousand three hundred eighty-seven.

Evening at Lourdes, in the south of France. A procession is forming, and candles are being lit all across the square. At the very front, before the bishops, before the choirs, come the wheelchairs. Old men in blankets. A girl with a breathing tube. A woman lying on a stretcher, looking up at the sky. Pushing them are volunteers in uniform, some of them teenagers, some of them doctors on vacation, some who were pushed in a chair themselves years ago. The crowd waits for them to pass. Nobody hurries them. At a shrine famous for hoped-for cures, what stands out is the order of the line. Today, who goes first.
screen: `CANDLES AT LOURDES.` → `WHEELCHAIRS AT THE FRONT.` → `VOLUNTEERS PUSHING.`

segments.voice: Lourdes in France and Fatima in Portugal are shrines tied to appearances of Mary that the Church has judged worthy of belief. Earlier on this path we met them as stories. Today, we meet them as pilgrims do. First, the sick at the center. At Lourdes, the sick are given the places of honor. They are seated at the front for Mass and processions, and the Eucharist is carried past them in blessing. Volunteers come from parishes and dioceses to push chairs, carry stretchers, help at the baths, and serve meals. Some go back year after year. Second, why. Jesus put it plainly in Matthew's Gospel, describing the judgment of the nations. Among the things the blessed did for him, he says, in the Douay-Rheims, "sick, and you visited me." At these shrines, Catholics are acting that verse out in public, with the whole crowd watching. Third, what about cures. Some pilgrims hope for healing, and the Church takes reports seriously. At Lourdes a medical office examines claims, and the Church is slow and careful before calling any cure a miracle. Some pilgrims speak of a different kind of healing: peace, courage, a family reconciled, a caregiver who finally rests. Fourth, Fatima. There, some pilgrims walk long distances to the shrine, pray the rosary together in different languages, and fill the square with candles at night. The sick are prayed for by name. Lourdes and Fatima differ in their stories. As pilgrimages, they share a center: the weakest in the crowd go first, and the strong push.
screen: `THE SICK GET THE PLACES OF HONOR.` · `SICK, AND YOU VISITED ME.` · `CURES ARE EXAMINED SLOWLY.` · `FATIMA: CANDLES AND THE ROSARY.` · then, large: `THE WEAKEST GO FIRST.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: help a sick person travel. Not to France. Maybe just across town. Settle, and breathe. Think of someone you know who is sick, frail, or stuck at home. A neighbor after surgery. A grandparent who no longer drives. A friend going through treatment. Picture where they would like to go and can't easily reach: a church, a doctor, a park, a grandchild's game. Picture yourself driving them, or walking slowly beside them, letting them set the pace. If you pray, you can hold them in prayer, and ask for the courage to offer. If you don't, just hold them in mind. The bell holds the time.
Lourdes and Fatima as pilgrims. Marian shrines where the sick are given the places of honor and volunteers serve them. Today's word.
screen: `LOURDES AND FATIMA AS PILGRIMS — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: the sick go first. Today, offer one sick or frail person a ride, a walk, or an errand, and let them set the pace. Day one thousand three hundred eighty-seven.

howItsDone: Dioceses and parishes organize pilgrimages to Lourdes and Fatima that bring sick people together with volunteer caregivers, nurses and doctors; the sick are seated first at Masses and processions and are prayed for and blessed.

fork.setup: you're a teenage volunteer at Lourdes. the evening procession is forming and you're pushing a man in a wheelchair. where does the procession put you?
options: at the very back, out of the way.
at the front, ahead of the crowd.
at the side, so he can watch.

trapdoor: what you thought: people go to Lourdes and Fatima hoping for miracles.
what it means: these are pilgrimages built around the sick, who go first, and the volunteers who serve them.
what a scholar hears: Matthew 25:36, sick, and you visited me, acted out in public; cures are examined carefully before any is called a miracle.
